entries.title: The Mystics Sure Look Ready for the Playoffs
entries.summary: Washington’s 93-77 win over Indiana was among its best performances of the year, boosting its playoff seeding.
entries.content:
The 2026 Mystics are young. Perhaps you’ve heard: It has been the defining theme of this season, popping up everywhere, the one piece of information found in any discussion about this roster. For much of the season, their average player age was scarcely 23, with their youth fully on display in their nicknames and dance routines and locker-room celebrations. They are the youngest roster to qualify for the playoffs in the history of the WNBA.

Yet that focus does them a bit of a disservice. This young team has grown up in some awfully important ways this year. And that development is obvious as they start looking ahead to the playoffs.

The Mystics’ 93-77 win over the Fever on Sunday was among their most complete performances of the year. In a game with major playoff seeding implications, Washington controlled the pace from the jump while shutting down the most potent offense in the league. It was an encouraging show of strength. The WNBA regular season wraps up next week, and the Fever represented the final real battle for the Mystics, whose schedule finishes with a pair of games against losing teams.

But if this was supposed to be one last, big test, Washington had all of the answers from the start.

“This is a young team that amazingly has a very clear idea of how we need to play together on both ends of the court,” Mystics coach Sydney Johnson said afterward. “I think that’s evident in how we play.”

It was hard to argue that point. And there’s certainly been plenty of individual player development here. Kiki Iriafen and Sonia Citron have both improved on their All-Star rookie seasons. Over the last two months, Georgia Amoore has found her scoring touch, and Lauren Betts has looked more comfortable and confident as she has polished her footwork.

The resident elder stateswoman around here, 26-year-old Shakira Austin, has unlocked personal bests in nearly every statistical category in her fifth season on the Mystics. (She left Sunday’s win with an apparent knee injury, but it doesn’t appear to be serious.)

“If she doesn't get Most Improved Player, I think I'm going to start a riot,” Amoore said on Sunday. “Like, a literal riot.”

But the most striking change over the last few months has been how those pieces fit together — which felt obvious against the Fever on Sunday. The Mystics offered a balanced offensive attack, with Iriafen, Austin, Citron and Amoore all scoring in double digits. Their ball movement was crisp and clean, and their defensive switches were nearly seamless. The collective impression was of a team who knows each other exceedingly well. And that felt especially true when facing a late push from the Fever.

In a choppy, disjointed third quarter, Indiana whittled a 26-point lead down to 14. The Mystics played a few possessions that felt jittery, with momentum swinging toward the Fever on a 30-foot three-pointer from Caitlin Clark, exactly the sort of play that sparks comebacks and sets crowds alight. Here, it was just an isolated highlight. The Mystics cleaned up and locked in. The score never drew any closer.

“Last year, or maybe even earlier this year, we would have been reeling from that,” Johnson said. “Not with this team. This team’s really grown up a lot and just learned to compose themselves.”

The win felt like a sign of how far they have come. Washington’s first two games against Indiana this season were decided by a combined four points back in May and June. It never felt close in September. The difference might be critical in the postseason seeding for these two teams.

The WNBA’s eight playoff teams have been set for weeks now. But there are still plenty of questions around how they might be paired up. The Mystics entered Sunday as the eighth seed and moved up to the seventh with their win over the Fever. But they could potentially finish as high as fourth. Just two games separate the No. 4 seed from the No. 8. And every team has two games left to play — meaning that nearly anything can happen in this race over the final week of the season. But the outlook is remarkably good for the Mystics.

They hold the head-to-head tiebreaker over three of these four teams. (The Mystics won their season series against the Dream, Fever and Wings, while they lost to the Liberty.) The three teams currently ahead of Washington face a brutal home stretch: The No. 4 Dream and No. 6 Liberty will play their final two games against each other, while the No. 5 Fever has to play two games against the No. 1 Lynx, who are motivated to lock in the top overall seed. But the No. 7 Mystics? Their last two games will come against losing teams.

Washington faces Connecticut on Tuesday and Chicago on Thursday. That last game will matter for more than just playoff seeding: The Mystics hold the rights to the Sky’s 2027 first-round draft pick. In other words, every additional loss for the Sky improves the chances of a high pick for the Mystics, which is especially valuable in a loaded draft class like the one expected next year.

But the mock drafts will have to wait. Plenty of young talent is here already. They have some more basketball left to play.

entries.title: Spirit 3, Chicago 0: Game Recap
entries.summary: Trinity Rodman notched a goal and an assist in a road win over the Stars.
entries.content:
Trinity Rodman scored in the seventh minute and added a late assist in the visiting Washington Spirit’s 3-0 victory over the Chicago Stars on Sunday.

In the day’s other National Women’s Soccer League matches, the Houston Dash edged the Boston Legacy 2-1, Angel City FC shut out the Utah Royals 3-0, and Bay FC defeated Racing Louisville 2-0.

Rodman provided an early spark, lifting a shot over Stars goalkeeper Alyssa Naeher in the seventh minute. She sealed the win 78 minutes later, sending a lofted cross to Tamara Bolt’s head for Washington’s final goal.

Andi Sullivan doubled the Spirit’s lead from the penalty spot in the 34th minute after Chicago’s Bea Franklin was called for a handball in the box. Sullivan placed the kick into the bottom left corner.

Chicago (5-18-2) outshot Washington 5-4 despite the Spirit (14-7-4) controlling nearly 60% of possession.

entries.title: FAA Launches AI Air Traffic Control Tool at D.C. Airports
entries.summary: Airports in the D.C.-area will be the first to use SMART, an AI-powered software aimed at “preventing disruptions.”
entries.content:
A new AI-powered air traffic control tool touted by the Trump administration as a way to reduce delays and offset overcrowded airspace launched at D.C.-area airports Monday.

The capital region airports — Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Washington Dulles International Airport and Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport — are the first to implement the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routing and Trajectories (SMART) software ahead of a nationwide rollout, according to a Monday statement from the Department of Transportation. The program uses AI to analyze data including weather patterns, flight paths and controller staffing levels to make recommendations to air traffic controllers and “prevent disruptions before they happen” by suggesting alternative routes when airspace is crowded.

The $875 million system is part of the administration’s push to modernize the nation's air-traffic infrastructure and is expected to be deployed nationwide by 2028. That $12.5 billion investment will upgrade communication lines and install new radars and radios. The new AI program will reshape airspace management by predicting congestion problems up to weeks in advance, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement.

“To really improve the flying experience for American people, we needed to build a 21st century scheduling tool like SMART,” Duffy said.

The Transportation Department has assured the SMART software will not replace human decision-making but rather support air traffic controllers by providing recommendations, not making final decisions about flight paths or controlling airplanes.

The Federal Aviation Administration currently has about 11,000 certified air traffic controllers with plans to increase the workforce to 12,563 by 2028. That’s down from the 14,633 it planned to hire for those years back in 2024.

Washington’s airspace is one of the busiest in the nation and has drawn scrutiny for years. There’s been a renewed effort to fix the jumbled flight corridor following a deadly January 2025 collision that killed 67 people at Reagan National Airport. A report from the National Transportation Safety Board faulted the FAA for various failures leading to the crash.

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Virginia), who co-sponsored recent legislation aimed to reduce the number of flights at Reagan National and address overcrowding, said AI is not going to fix the problem.

“The National Transportation Safety Board issued 50 safety recommendations in the wake of the tragic midair collision near DCA—and none have been fully implemented yet,” he said. “Instead of cutting corners with new AI proposals, our immediate focus should be on those recommendations, the need to reduce flight traffic in and out of DCA, and reauthorizing the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law so we can modernize and staff up our air traffic control towers and networks.”

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement the new software, in combination with ongoing physical upgrades, will maintain a “gold standard of safety” across the nation.

The Trump administration also plugged potentially lower ticker prices thanks to SMART, which it said will help airlines waste less fuel and reduce staff overtime, passing on savings to customers.

entries.title: State Department: Strait of Hormuz Is Still ‘Unreliable and Dangerous’
entries.summary: Trump has repeatedly claimed the strait is “open.”
entries.content:
The State Department is resupplying the U.S. Embassy in Kuwait via “alternative routes” because transit through the Strait of Hormuz is “unreliable and dangerous,” according to a contracting notice the department posted Sunday.

“The security situation in the region remains fluid and subject to sudden escalation,” the department wrote in a vendor notice posted to a government contracting website — a statement undercutting President Donald Trump’s assertions that the strait is open and under U.S. control.

As recently as last week, Trump claimed that the Iranian navy was “gone” and the strait was open for business.

“You watch what's gonna happen to Iran, it’s gonna be a really good conclusion,” Trump said at a rally in North Carolina on Wednesday. “We have the strait open, we have all this thing and they've been decimated. Their navy’s gone, their air force is gone.”

It’s hardly the first time Trump has made such a proclamation:

“We control the strait, 100%.”

“We have total control over the strait. … The strait is open.”’

“The strait is open. We take a lot of ships through the strait now. … It’s a very functioning strait.”

The claims, made by the president on Aug. 10, 17 and 26, respectively, are just some of those highlighted by the White House as it tries to convince the American public that it is winning the deeply unpopular war.
HormuzMap (1164x871, AR: 1.34)The State Department said in the vendor notice that it considered three vendors before choosing one capable of transporting freight to the U.S. Embassy in Kuwait via unspecified “alternative routes,” as regional instability rendered “standard shipping routes unreliable or unavailable.” That embassy is located near the Persian Gulf’s northern shore, in close proximity to Iran.

A few ships passed through the strait this weekend, NBC News reported, but shipping traffic is only a fraction of what’s considered normal during peacetime.

“Recurring, rapid changes in regional security conditions are affecting carrier availability, shipping routes, transit times, insurance requirements, and overall logistics reliability with little advance notice,” the notice reads.

The selected contractor — the government did not disclose its identity — quoted $26,908 for its services and has a “strong record of relevant past performance supporting U.S. Embassy Kuwait requirements.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment. The State Department referred questions to U.S. Central Command, which directed The Washington Sun to its social media account.
Hormuz.ships (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)The United States first attacked Iran on Feb. 28; next week, the war will hit its seven-month mark. Trump cut short a trip to Camp David this weekend as he weighs his next moves in his war, saying he may “blow the entire nation up.”

The Kuwait Embassy and others in the region issued security alerts on Saturday, warning of the Houthis’ “hostilities against Saudi Arabia” and writing, “This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly.”

Iran, for its part, warned Monday that it would consider expanding “the geography” of the war if the United States escalated attacks. Meanwhile, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to travel to New York City on Tuesday for the United Nations General Assembly, and Trump has suggested that he’s willing to meet with Pezeshkian.

entries.title: Federal Judge Limits ICE Agents in Construction Site Searches and Detentions
entries.summary: The ruling sides with a U.S. citizen, twice detained in warrantless worksite raids and held even after he showed Alabama REAL ID.
entries.content:
A federal judge in Alabama on Monday temporarily barred immigration officers from entering construction sites without a warrant and detaining workers without suspicion that they live in the country illegally.

The order from U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Beaverstock, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, sides with Leo Garcia Venegas, a U.S. citizen and construction worker whom immigration agents have detained three times in Alabama since the beginning of Trump’s second term.

Immigration agents detained Venegas while on the job at private construction sites 20 miles apart, once on May 21, 2025, and again on June 12, 2025, even though he showed his Alabama REAL ID, according to court documents filed in the lawsuit. Agents detained Venegas a third time in his driveway on May 2.

Beaverstock’s order concludes that the government’s actions against Venegas likely violated the Constitution. While the case moves forward, Beaverstock is barring agents from entering construction sites without warrants or consent; from detaining workers without suspicion that each of them resides in the U.S. illegally; and from continuing the detention of those who present documents showing their lawful status.

The judge pointed out that the government provided “little in the way of response” to an argument from Venegas’ attorneys that an Alabama REAL ID should not be ignored as preemptive proof of citizenship.

“The record also reflects that Venegas was not promptly released following the production of his REAL ID to officers,” Beaverstock wrote. “Instead, the officers disregarded the veracity of his documentation and continued to detain him. A policy that permits such action is likely to run afoul of the Fourth Amendment.”

The judge also was not convinced by Justice Department arguments that the agents didn’t need a warrant to enter a construction site.

“The nature of the worksite does not open the floodgates to warrantless government intrusion and there exists no justification to enter a construction site that is not open to the public to conduct warrantless seizure,” Beaverstock wrote.

Venegas, who sued the Department of Homeland Security nearly a year ago, says he’s traumatized after the repeated detentions.

“For the first time in a long time, I will be able to go to work without worrying that I will be arrested for no reason,” he said in a statement. “Americans cannot be stopped and held by law enforcement when they are doing nothing wrong.”

DHS denied to the court that such policies existed. Beaverstock admonished the government for not putting forward arguments to explain why Venegas’ detentions didn’t violate the law.

“The Government’s position that the safety of the officers was a factor is unsupported by the record especially given that there were multiple individuals on the jobsite who did not appear to be Hispanic, and none of those individuals were detained in the name of safety,” he wrote. “Finally, the Government offers no factual support whatsoever as to why officers reasonably believed Venegas ‘may be an alien.’”

entries.title: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker Reveals He Uses a GLP-1 Medication
entries.summary: The potential 2028 presidential contender said he has struggled his “whole life” to lose weight.
entries.content:
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) revealed for the first time on Monday that he has been taking a GLP-1 medication for weight loss and has lost 80 pounds so far.

“I have an opportunity, just with the platform that I have as governor, to tell people that this is something that can work for them,” Pritzker said in an interview with CBS News. “I think they should do it with the doctor's advice, but I can tell you, at least for me, it has been really life-changing.”

Illinois’ state employees also have GLP-1s covered on their insurance plans, a policy Pritzker said will save the state money because “people will be less overweight, which causes so many other diseases.”

The Illinois governor previously remained mum about the reason behind his weight loss, telling Politico in August 2025, “how about, just for health,” when he was asked about being noticeably slimmer.

Pritzker, who is widely considered a potential 2028 presidential candidate, was diagnosed with diabetes two years ago. The two-term governor brushed off a question from CBS News’ David Begnaud about whether using a GLP-1 had anything to do with cultivating his image so he can run for president.

“I've been driven my whole life to lose weight,” Pritzker replied — adding that he has “not made any decisions” about what offices he’ll pursue in the future because he is focused on seeking his third term as Illinois governor.

Pritzker said his father died suddenly at the age of 39 while playing tennis, and “he was actually quite an active person, even though he was overweight.”

Pritzker said he had been overweight for most of his life, but the high pressure governor’s gig caused him to put on more weight, which led to negative attention.

President Donald Trump called Pritzker a “big, fat slob” in November 2025 as he talked about sending National Guard troops to Chicago to combat crime and make it a “safe city” — a policy Pritzker strongly opposed.

entries.title: Venezuelan DoorDash Driver Recounts Being Shot by an ICE Officer
entries.summary: “I was telling him it hurt a lot, that I couldn’t move,” Wilber Rafael Garces Perez said during a press conference from detention.
entries.content:
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, the Venezuelan man shot by a federal immigration agent on Sunday, said he is now in detention but still has the bullet in his back.

The 28-year-old man, who was in the middle of a DoorDash delivery in Austin, Texas, when he was shot, spoke by phone to reporters during a news conference Monday. He said doctors didn’t remove the bullet from his back because it was close to his spine and that federal officials were in a hurry to take him into detention.

“I said, ‘How are you going to leave the bullet there if it hurts?’” Garces Perez said in Spanish.

Garces Perez said an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent instructed him to exit his car on Sunday. He replied that he didn’t want to leave his car in the middle of the road. Then, he said he took a U-turn to find parking, an ICE agent sideswiped his car and he was shot.

“I was telling him it hurt a lot, that I couldn’t move. I was basically passed out,” Garces Perez said in Spanish.

Garces Perez went to the hospital for treatment but did not undergo surgery to remove the bullet. ICE took him to the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall at 4 a.m., which is about 140 miles south of the city, said immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, who is representing Garces Perez.

Lincoln-Goldfinch filed a petition on Monday in federal court seeking Garces Perez’s release from ICE custody, according to a court docket.

The Department of Homeland Security said it is investigating the officer-involved shooting of “an illegal alien from Venezuela.” Garces Perez entered the country during President Joe Biden’s administration and “had a final order of removal,” DHS said.

Garces Perez entered the country in 2024 as an asylum seeker and had a work permit, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. He received a removal order after missing a court date because the notice of the hearing was sent to an old address, the attorney said.

Reps. Lloyd Doggett and Greg Casar, both Democrats from Texas, spoke about the need for accountability during the press conference before Garces Perez spoke. Casar said he wouldn’t allow ICE to deport Garces Perez.

“Congress is making it very clear to the head of ICE and to Secretary [Markwayne] Mullin that Wilber Garces needs to be released to medical care and should not be in Pearsall,” Casar said. “He needs to be released right now.”

entries.title: With Daniels’ Timeline Unclear, the Commanders Will Start Marcus Mariota in Week 3
entries.summary: The Commanders quarterback will consult specialists this week after dislocating his elbow on Sunday.
entries.content:
Backup quarterback Marcus Mariota will be the Commanders’ starter for their home opener Sunday against the Seahawks, coach Dan Quinn announced on Monday. Mariota will replace Jayden Daniels, who dislocated his left elbow in Sunday’s loss to the Cowboys.

Quinn said Daniels had some imaging done on the elbow Monday and will consult specialists this week as the team maps out a timeline for his return.

Daniels went down on the final play of the first half in Sunday’s 37-20 loss to the Cowboys. The quarterback’s foot was stepped on by left guard Chris Paul and he stumbled out of the snap, dislocating his elbow in the fall. He stayed down on the turf for an extended period as his teammates headed to the locker room for the halftime break.

When asked Monday about the level of concern with Daniels’ elbow after previous injuries involving the quarterback’s left arm, Quinn said he just feels bad that his quarterback keeps having to deal with these setbacks.

“[It] sucks for him,” Quinn said. “I know how much these guys put into it, and so when there's setbacks like this you just want to stand by him as close as you can on this detour to getting back onto the field.”

As far as replacing Daniels, Quinn said that with Mariota being in his third season in Washington, he doesn’t foresee any “pullback” to the playbook when the 12-year veteran steps in against Seattle.

“We're fortunate in that way, that he's put in all the same timelines and guidelines with the players,” Quinn said of Mariota. “So it won't be exactly the same, but fortunately they'll have a lot of similarities.”

Sunday’s somber scene was similar to one from last November when Daniels first dislocated his elbow in a 38-14 Week 9 loss to the Seahawks. The Commanders were down 38-7 when Daniels’ elbow was bent back during a fourth-quarter tackle, leading to questions about why Washington’s star player was still on the field.

Daniels missed four weeks with the dislocation, returning Dec. 7 to face the Vikings. He was unable to finish that game, leaving in the second half after landing on the same elbow. With Washington no longer in playoff contention, he was ruled out for the final four games of 2025.

That decision marked the end of a nightmarish sophomore season for Daniels, who ultimately missed 10 games with injuries. In his absence, Mariota threw for 1,695 yards, 10 touchdowns and seven interceptions while completing 61% of his passes. The Commanders went 2-6 in the eight games Mariota started.

In replacement duty on Sunday, Mariota went 11 of 16 for 111 yards and a touchdown.

Just two weeks into a new year, Daniels is the second key starter to go down for Washington. Left tackle Laremy Tunsil is expected to miss most of the season with a torn triceps.

entries.title: Federal Reserve Official Says Fighting Inflation Likely To Be 'Painful'
entries.content:
By Christopher Rugaber

WASHINGTON (AP) — A top Federal Reserve official said Monday that the central bank may have to cause economic pain in the form of higher unemployment to combat stubbornly high inflation.

Austan Goolsbee, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, said in a speech in London that the Fed is facing a series of persistent supply shocks that have driven up inflation, including higher oil prices from the Iran war and tariffs. Typically, Goolsbee noted, the central bank would essentially wait for such shocks to fade and inflation to fall on its own rather than raise borrowing costs.

But faced with an ongoing series of persistent supply shocks, the Fed now has little choice but to hike rates, Goolsbee said. The increases are needed to lower consumer and business demand to a level consistent with reduced supply, he added, which should bring inflation back to the Fed's 2% target.

“The only way to bring inflation down is to raise rates and narrow the gap between supply and demand,” he said in a written copy of his remarks. “Forcing inflation back to target in the short run means pushing employment below target. ... In the short run, supply shocks force a difficult trade-off” between the Fed's goals of low inflation and maximum employment.

“It’s going to be painful,” Goolsbee said in later to reporters. “It would necessarily be painful.”

Goolsbee's comments contradict Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's remarks last Wednesday at a news conference that took place after the Fed lifted its key interest rate for the first time in three years to about 3.9%.

“I don’t believe that we need to do harm to the labor markets to achieve our objective,” Warsh said last week.

The Fed generally fights inflation by raising interest rates to cool borrowing and spending. Historically, such rate hikes have often slowed growth and have even led to recessions.

Yet in 2022-2023, the Fed sharply raised interest rates and inflation did decline, without a significant rise in unemployment or economic slowdown.

Goolsbee also suggested while speaking with reporters that the Fed may need to implement more than just the one additional rate hike later this year that policymakers, as a group, forecast last week.

There are signs that surging investment in data centers for AI are also pushing up inflation, he said, suggesting that strong demand is playing a role, as well as the supply shock from oil.

If inflation mostly comes from supply shocks, then just one more rate hike could be sufficient, Goolsbee told reporters.

“And if we get evidence that convinces us that it’s coming from demand, then it likely would not be enough,” he said.

entries.title: Air Traffic Equipment Failure Sparks Massive Flight Delays
entries.summary: Travel in and out of the Philadelphia, New York and New Jersey areas was delayed by as much as four hours.
entries.content:
More than 500 flights have been canceled out of Newark Liberty International on Monday, with severe disruptions rippling throughout the United States after a construction crew mistakenly severed a “massive” telecom line in New Jersey, causing some air traffic communications systems to falter.

Departures and arrivals were initially delayed from two to three hours on average out of Philadelphia International Airport, LaGuardia Airport, John F. Kennedy International Airport, Newark and Teterboro Airport. The interruptions have postponed 241 flights at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, with average departure delays reaching 42 minutes as of 4:45 p.m. Monday.

By that time, about 1,785 flights had been canceled nationwide, about five times more than this year’s daily average.

The FAA issued the ground stop notice following a radio and communications failure at the Philadelphia TRACON air traffic control facility. When air traffic controllers switched to a backup system, they discovered that an Amtrak construction crew had accidentally cut into a fiber optic line in New Jersey, FAA officials said.

The accident triggered a widespread communications outage that forced the FAA to pause flights in the Northeast, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said.

“That fiber break is probably 13 hours to repair. It’s massive,” Bedford told CBS.

Officials estimated repairs could continue into Tuesday morning.

At around 2:50 p.m., Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that operations were set to resume out of La Guardia and Philadelphia but flights from Newark, JFK and Teterboro Airport were still paused.

“This incident underscores the need for additional funding to modernize aging infrastructure and prevent disruptions like this in the future,” Duffy wrote Monday on X.

Last week, Bedford asked Congress for an additional $10 billion to modernize the nation's “aging and unreliable” air traffic control system, which has contributed to increased flight delays in recent years.

This story has been updated with further information on the delays and cancellations.

entries.title: A Vermont Man is Convicted of Attempted Murder for Shooting Three Palestinian Students
entries.summary: Jason Eaton could face life in prison in the November 2023 attack near the University of Vermont campus in Burlington.
entries.content:
By Michael R. Sisak and Amanda Swinhart

A jury on Monday convicted a Vermont man of attempted murder in the shootings of three Palestinian college students who were walking near his home, rejecting an insanity defense rooted in his claims that he was acting on orders from the CIA and Mossad.

Jason Eaton, 51, faces up to life in prison in the November 2023 attack near the University of Vermont campus in Burlington, which left Hisham Awartani paralyzed from the waist down and his friends, Tahseen Aliahmad and Kinnan Abdalhamid, wounded.

The jury deliberated for several hours before reaching its verdict after a weeklong trial that saw testimony from the three wounded men and psychiatric experts called by the defense and prosecution.

Eaton was ordered jailed pending sentencing, which has yet to be scheduled. He stared ahead blankly as the verdict was read. Awartani and Aliahmad, sitting in the front row of the courtroom gallery, smiled and hugged people around them.

Eaton had pleaded not guilty but did not dispute that he was the shooter. His lawyers argued that he should be found not guilty by reason of insanity, pointing to his claims that the U.S. and Israeli intelligence agencies transmitted orders to shoot the men to him via FM radio and that God was commanding him to protect his Jewish neighbors.

Had he been found not guilty by reason of insanity, he could have been ordered to undergo mental health treatment.

The shooting, a few days after Thanksgiving, shook Burlington, Vermont, and reverberated in the West Bank, where the three wounded men grew up and became friends as schoolmates in Ramallah before moving to the U.S. for college.

The November 2023 shooting, weeks after the start of the Israel-Hamas war, spawned calls for a hate crime investigation.

But no hate crime charges were filed as questions persisted about whether anti-Palestinian animus, an altered mental state or something else had compelled Eaton to open fire on Awartani, Aliahmad and Abdalhamid, who were all 20 at the time.

Eaton’s lawyers argued he was suffering from a delusional, psychotic disorder after losing his job at a credit union two weeks before the shooting.

While listening to a local NPR affiliate, Eaton believed he was hearing messages he attributed to the CIA, defense lawyer Joshua O’Hara said. At first, the messages were encouraging and validating, the lawyer said, but subsequent messages turned dark, insisting that Eaton “has to go out and shoot somebody.”

Authorities found three shotguns in Eaton’s apartment and a Ruger .380-caliber handgun that crime lab testing concluded was the gun used in the shooting, prosecutor Sally Adams said. Eaton had purchased the gun seven months earlier from a Vermont gun store.

Awartani, Aliahmad and Abdalhamid, all of whom are now 23, told jurors of their holiday weekend visit to Awartani’s grandmother’s house, a trip to a bowling alley to celebrate his twin cousins’ birthday, and the walk they took near the University of Vermont campus after dusk that ended in bloodshed.

Awartani, who was studying at Brown University in Rhode Island at the time, said they were smoking cigarettes and speaking a mix of English and Arabic. Two of them said they were wearing traditional Palestinian scarves known as keffiyehs. Awartani said he first noticed Eaton standing on a porch as they approached the apartment house where he lived.

Within seconds, Awartani said, Eaton was off the porch and walking toward them. His face was expressionless and he didn’t say anything. As Eaton got to about five to 10 feet (1.5 to 3 meters) away, “he pulled out a handgun and started shooting at us,” said Awartani, who was paralyzed from the waist down in the shooting and now uses a wheelchair.

Jacob Pyne, who lived in a different apartment in the same house as Eaton, testified that he heard four to six gunshots, followed by footsteps going up the stairs of the apartment house. He said he ran outside and heard two men speaking, one of whom was more vocal and yelling, “I’ve been shot, help me.” He then brought the men blankets and called 911.

Abdalhamid, a student at Haverford College near Philadelphia, said he fled and hid behind another home after seeing Aliahmad fall to the ground. He said he only realized later when he sat down that he had also been wounded. Awartani was shot in the chest and the bullet ricocheted off his scapula, causing paraplegia in his spinal cord. Aliahmad, who was a student at Trinity College in Connecticut, was struck in the collarbone, and Abdalhamid was shot in the right buttock.

entries.title: Trump and Mamdani Focus on Housing at Their New York Meetup
entries.summary: The pair agreed to “set up a new level of that conversation” between City Hall and the White House on housing development for New York.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani told reporters on Monday that they focused on housing development for the city during their meeting at Gracie Mansion, the mayor’s official residence.

For decades, New York officials have floated developing 140 acres at Sunnyside Yard, which serves as an active rail yard for Amtrak, New Jersey Transit and the Long Island Rail Road in western Queens.

“We've spoken about Sunnyside Yard,” Mamdani announced at a news conference, “and it's a real pleasure that just today we've agreed to set up a new level of that conversation between our housing and operations team at City Hall and the White House team, because what we're speaking about is 12,000 homes, 30,000 jobs, the prospect of an entire new neighborhood in a city where housing is the number one cost.”.

Trump called the Sunnyside Yard development a “big job” he has been watching for 35 years.

“I would say that was a very federal-oriented job,” Trump said at the news conference. “You're going to need a lot of federal approvals and probably some federal money to do it, but it's always been a great location.”

The meeting marked the first time Trump visited Gracie Mansion as a sitting president. Trump said he encouraged Mamdani to live in the mansion even though the mayor had doubts about moving in because “it is a little bit on the luxurious side.”

When asked about affordability, a term Trump has deemed a “hoax” in the past, the president said he knew “a lot about affordability” because he developed “many low-income and moderate-income buildings over the years, and had great success with it.” A development at Sunnyside Yards would have to have “a pretty substantial component of exactly that,” Trump added.

When Trump and Mamdani met at the White House in February, Mamdani proposed “securing more than $21 billion in federal grants to construct the world’s largest deck over the site” in order to allow the housing development project to begin.

Mamdani and Trump's remarks come as the president’s ban on several news outlets from entering the White House grounds remains in effect.

The mayor said that he stressed that it is important to engage with all members of the press “no matter the opinion or the critique,” while Trump lambasted the banned news services as being “very bad for national security” and publishing “biased news.”

entries.title: Some Midwest Republicans Are Calling to End the Iran War to Ease Fuel Prices
entries.summary: Members of Congress push for ending the war in Iran or cutting diesel exports as prices soar.
entries.content:
Rep. Ashley Hinson on Monday called for the U.S. war with Iran to be “brought to a successful and immediate end” as diesel prices soar to their highest recorded average.

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Hinson, an Iowa Republican now running for Senate, wrote on X. “We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices.”

Hinson said the government should suspend the gas tax and begin “unleashing E-15” — a fuel source that contains more ethanol made from corn.

The Iowa Republican also called for pausing diesel exports, reinstating biodiesel tax credits and “creating a diesel relief program to help our farmers and truckers being crushed by the high costs.”

Diesel prices hit $6.51 on Monday, which is the highest recorded average price according to AAA fuel price tracker.

Iowa's farming industry has been under strain as the Iran war drives up the price of fertilizers and fuel. The state ranks second for the value of its agricultural sector production, according to September data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Farm Income and Wealth Statistics.

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee for Michigan Senate, also called for the war in Iran to end and released an ad on Monday that pushed for policies to alleviate the recent economic strain, including a temporary embargo on diesel exports until the end of the conflict.

Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) also called on President Donald Trump to halt diesel exports — comparing the need for the move to Richard Nixon’s 1973 temporary embargo on exports of soybeans, cottonseed and related products to curb inflation and shortages.

“High diesel prices ARE KILLING FARMERS INCOME,” Grassley wrote in a post on X.

Grassley argued that if the government can put an embargo on selling software chips to China, then the U.S. can also impose export controls on diesel. The Iowa senator said that oil companies, that have pushed against an embargo on diesel exports, should at least accept lower profit margins from their domestic sales to farmers.

Family farmers need to be “on the strongest footing possible no matter what’s happening across the globe,” Grassley said.

Hinson and Grassley have voted against war powers resolutions that would limit Trump’s ability to take action in the war with Iran without seeking congressional approval.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters last week that he would be open to considering a diesel export ban if it could lower the fuel prices.

Trump last month accused Exxon Mobil and Chevron of “making too much money” after the companies reported strong quarterly earnings in their recent reports. The president called for the energy companies to “cut the retail price” of their products to help Americans at the gas pump.

entries.title: White House to Announce ‘Trump TV’ Days After Press Ban
entries.summary: The new venture comes just days after President Trump barred three major media organizations from the White House.
entries.content:
The White House is set to launch its own news channel dubbed “Trump TV,” days after President Donald Trump banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.

An announcement detailing the channel is scheduled for 7 p.m. Monday on the White House’s YouTube channel

“Watch the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place,” the announcement said. “Top videos, major remarks, and must-see highlights streaming 24/7 and updated in real time. Stay informed and stay up to date!”

The banned media outlets responded with a federal lawsuit against the Trump administration following the president’s announcement on Friday. Trump warned that more “fake news” outlets could be blacklisted in the coming days.

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States,” he wrote on Truth Social. 

The White House did not immediately respond to The Washington Sun’s request for comment, and has provided no further details about the Trump TV announcement.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

entries.title: Appeals Court Revives Missouri’s Republican-Friendly Congressional Map Push
entries.summary: The decision, which is set to be appealed, gives Republicans another shot at the map they drew this year.
entries.content:
A federal appeals court in Missouri sided with Republicans on Monday afternoon, breathing new life into the party’s push for a more GOP-friendly U.S. House map in the state.

“This sounds so crazy because the ballots have already been printed,” Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, a Democrat whose district was split up by the Republican-favored map, said when The Washington Sun told him of the decision. “Some people have voted.”

Just a week ago, the issue of which map Missourians would use in November seemed all but settled. The Supreme Court had blocked an order from a lower court that required state officials to use the new map.

But the federal appeals court flipped that Monday, ruling that the lower court should enforce that order in seven days unless the Supreme Court steps in. This tees up another emergency appeal to the high court, and People Not Politicians, the advocacy group opposed to the redistricting push, has pledged to do so.

It will be the third time the court has dealt with Missouri’s redistricting efforts this year, in two separate cases. In the latest, on Sep. 10, the high court stopped Republicans from using the new congressional districts in a one-page order that did not include a reason for the decision and had no noted dissents.

The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruling comes after Missouri began sending out its mail-in ballots to absentee voters on Friday based on the 2022 congressional map, which was left in place in a separate case where the Supreme Court rejected an emergency appeal.

In its Monday decision, the 8th Circuit wrote that using the 2025 redrawn map would lead to the “least amount of confusion for voters subjected to a string of changes this month.”

Missouri was the second state to redraw its congressional map after President Donald Trump called on Republican legislatures to redraw their district lines in favor of Republicans. Almost exactly a year ago, Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe signed the “Missouri First” map into law aimed at netting Republicans one more U.S House seat, setting off a slew of lawsuits against the redraw.

The map targeted Cleaver’s district, splitting Kansas City into three different congressional districts.

In Missouri, laws passed by the legislature can be put to a voter referendum by collecting a certain number of signatures. People Not Power submitted the signatures to Secretary of State Denny Hoskins in December, but Hoskins waited until August 4, the same day as the state’s primary elections, to announce he would not be certifying the petition.

“Ballots have been printed, and Missourians have already voted,” Richard von Glahn, the executive director of People Not Politicians, wrote in a statement.

“Thousands more will vote before this order seeks to take effect. Officials should stop wasting taxpayers’ money on pointless legal action and instead focus on administering our elections. Missourians are already voting and will continue to vote no on Proposition A through November 3.”

This story has been updated with further information on the legal challenges.
